title: Wall Street Under Pressure as Oil Tops $105 and Treasury Yields Near 4.95%
intro:
US stocks fell for a fourth consecutive session as escalating tensions between the United States and Iran pushed oil prices above $105 a barrel. The 10-year Treasury yield approached 4.95%, reaching its highest level since 2023 and adding pressure on the Nasdaq and growth stocks.
Investors are now turning their attention to the US CPI report, which could further strengthen expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike next week.

Wall Street: Fourth Consecutive Decline
Pressure on US equities intensified, with the major Wall Street indexes closing lower for a fourth straight session.
The S&P 500 fell 0.58% to 7,591.70, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.60% to 52,064.10. The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.65% to 26,081.72.
The four-day decline represents the S&P 500's weakest stretch since June. The index is now roughly 2% below its August 13 record high, highlighting the gradual reduction in risk appetite following the recent market highs.
The key driver, however, is not equities alone. The latest move needs to be viewed through an increasingly fragile intermarket backdrop characterized by higher oil prices, rising Treasury yields and expectations for tighter monetary policy.

Oil: Brent Above $105 as Geopolitical Risk Returns
The energy market remains the primary catalyst.
Brent crude traded above $105–108 a barrel, while WTI approached $103, putting the benchmark on track for a weekly gain of more than 12%, its strongest weekly increase since mid-July.
The escalation of the US-Iran conflict has revived concerns about prolonged disruptions to global energy supplies, particularly amid renewed risks surrounding tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The market is therefore not simply pricing a temporary supply disruption. The bigger concern is that a prolonged conflict could turn the current geopolitical premium in oil into a more persistent inflationary shock.
Reports surrounding the conflict indicate that some US officials have warned President Donald Trump that the war could continue through the remainder of his term, which ends in January 2029. At the same time, Tehran reportedly remains determined to continue fighting despite the growing economic costs.
The risk for financial markets is straightforward: the longer oil remains above $100, the greater the possibility that the energy shock feeds into headline inflation and, eventually, inflation expectations.

Treasuries: 10-Year Yield Nears 4.95%
The second major source of pressure is coming from the bond market.
The 10-year US Treasury yield moved toward 4.90–4.95%, levels not seen since 2023.
The move is particularly important for equities because it is occurring alongside the sharp rise in oil prices.
In other words, Wall Street is facing a double headwind: higher oil increases inflationary pressure, while higher Treasury yields raise the cost of capital and reduce the present value of future earnings.
This dynamic is particularly negative for growth and technology stocks, which tend to be more sensitive to changes in interest rates.
The US Treasury's expanded buyback operation also failed to reverse the move. Purchases came in below expectations, leaving the bond market under continued pressure.

US Inflation: PPI Strengthens the Case for a More Restrictive Fed
The August producer-price data added another layer of pressure.
The Producer Price Index (PPI) rose 0.4% month over month, matching expectations, but the market interpreted the result in the context of higher energy costs caused by the Iran conflict.
Markets are now pricing roughly a 71% probability of a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike next week, up from around 61% before the PPI release.
Attention now turns to the August US CPI report, which could become the week's key market catalyst.
A stronger-than-expected inflation reading, particularly if core inflation remains sticky, could reinforce expectations that the Federal Reserve will need to maintain a restrictive policy stance for longer.
For equities, therefore, the issue is not simply whether the Fed hikes rates next week. The bigger risk is that higher oil prices and persistent inflation prevent the Fed from shifting toward a more accommodative stance in the months ahead.

Technology: Nvidia and Micron Under Pressure
The technology sector was hit by the rise in Treasury yields.
Nvidia fell approximately 2.3%, while Micron suffered a sharper decline of around 4.7%.
The combination of higher yields and profit-taking across high-valuation AI stocks has increased volatility within the sector.
The move is particularly significant because it comes at a time when investors have already priced in very strong expectations for AI-related earnings growth.
Not all technology names followed the same path, however.
Apple gained around 3.6% following the launch of its new $1,999 foldable iPhone Duo, significantly outperforming the broader technology sector.

Industrials and Materials: Freeport-McMoRan Falls
The industrial and materials sectors also came under pressure.
Freeport-McMoRan declined following a Reuters report casting doubt on plans to expand tariffs to refined copper.
The tariff issue remains particularly important for industrial metals, where changes in US trade policy can quickly alter expectations for demand, margins and pricing.
Overall, materials and industrial stocks weakened alongside the broader deterioration in market sentiment.

Defense: AeroVironment Continues to Outperform
One of the strongest areas of the market remains defense and unmanned systems.
AeroVironment gained around 4.45%, supported by record revenue and a strong backlog.
The sector continues to attract investor interest as geopolitical tensions increase demand expectations for defense spending, autonomous systems and drones.
In an environment defined by elevated geopolitical uncertainty, the relative strength of defense stocks remains one of the clearest sector trends in the market.

Consumer Staples: Investors Seek Defensive Exposure
The Consumer Staples sector showed greater resilience.
Philip Morris International, Constellation Brands, Altria Group and Tyson Foods were among the stronger performers.
The move reflects a typical pattern during periods of rising uncertainty: when volatility, yields and geopolitical risks increase, investors tend to favor companies with relatively stable demand and lower sensitivity to the economic cycle.
The internal rotation within the market is therefore becoming increasingly important. While technology and materials are under pressure, defensive segments continue to show relative strength.


Consumer and Retail: Increasing Selectivity
The consumer space was far from uniformly defensive.
Cooper Companies plunged nearly 15% after cutting its full-year guidance.
American Eagle Outfitters fell almost 14%, highlighting continued pressure across selected retail and discretionary consumer names.
These moves show that the market is becoming increasingly selective. Simply belonging to a defensive or consumer sector is no longer enough. Earnings guidance, margins and future growth expectations are once again driving individual stock performance.


After Hours: Oracle Surges, Adobe More Cautious
The after-hours session delivered mixed signals from the software and cloud sectors.
Oracle gained roughly 4% after beating expectations. Adjusted EPS came in at $1.92, versus $1.74 expected, while revenue reached $19.35 billion, above the $19.14 billion consensus.
The biggest highlight was cloud infrastructure growth, which surged 121% to $7.4 billion.
Adobe, meanwhile, reacted more cautiously despite beating quarterly estimates. Adjusted EPS came in at $6.13, versus $6.08 expected, while revenue reached $6.76 billion, compared with $6.69 billion expected.
The problem was forward guidance, with fourth-quarter revenue expectations coming in softer than anticipated.
The message from the market is clear: beating estimates is not necessarily enough when future expectations are being revised lower.


Gold: $4,300 Under Pressure from Rising Yields
The outlook for gold has become more complicated.
The precious metal traded around $4,300 an ounce after falling nearly 2% in the previous session.
Higher Treasury yields represent a significant headwind for gold because the metal generates no interest income. As yields rise, the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets increases.
At the same time, gold remains caught between two opposing forces: geopolitical risk and safe-haven demand on one side, and higher yields and expectations for tighter Fed policy on the other.
Gold is now on track to lose more than 2% this week, which would mark its third consecutive weekly decline.


FX: Dollar Relatively Soft, Yen Recovers
The foreign-exchange market is showing a less straightforward picture than equities.
The US dollar is showing relative intraday weakness against higher-beta currencies, while the Japanese yen is recovering.
USD/JPY remains under pressure around 154, with support around 153.90 and 153.50, while initial resistance stands near 154.62.
GBP/JPY is also retreating toward 208, reflecting the yen's relative strength.
Among the commodity-linked currencies, the New Zealand dollar is the strongest performer, while the Australian dollar is also holding a positive bias.
The Canadian dollar, meanwhile, remains more vulnerable to oil-price volatility. The WTI pullback toward the $101 area has limited CAD strength, keeping USD/CAD above 1.3820.


Intermarket: The Real Risk Is Oil Plus Yields
The most important signal from the latest session comes from the intermarket relationship.
It is not oil alone that represents a problem for Wall Street. And it is not Treasury yields alone.
The real risk comes from the combination of the two moving higher at the same time.
If Brent remains firmly above $105–108 while the 10-year Treasury yield consolidates around 4.90–4.95%, markets could increasingly price in a scenario of more persistent inflation and a more restrictive Federal Reserve.
That would create a particularly challenging environment for the Nasdaq and high-growth stocks, while defensive, energy and defense sectors could continue to show relative strength.
Conversely, a cooling in oil prices combined with falling Treasury yields would quickly reduce pressure on risk assets.


Outlook: CPI Becomes the Next Major Catalyst
With Wall Street already coming off four consecutive negative sessions, investors are entering the CPI release with a more fragile positioning.
The inflation report will be important not only for rate expectations but also for determining whether the energy shock is beginning to alter the trajectory of US inflation.
Bullish scenario: CPI comes in below expectations, Treasury yields decline and oil stabilizes. Under this scenario, US indexes could attempt a rebound, particularly the Nasdaq.
Bearish scenario: CPI comes in above expectations, the 10-year yield moves toward or above 5%, and Brent remains above $105. In this case, the risk of another correction in US equities would increase significantly.
For now, the bias remains cautious.
The equity market can still rebound, but as long as oil prices and Treasury yields continue to rise together, the risk/reward profile for growth stocks remains less attractive.
The next major market catalyst is therefore the US CPI report ,not simply because of the inflation number itself, but because of the reaction across Treasury yields, the US dollar, oil and the Nasdaq.
